Triggers.value: Someone getting emotionally close to me

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I feel on guard even inside my own home

I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel intense shame

I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: 'Explosion or bang sounds' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is additional history not represented elsewhere. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal/home-based threat, emotional closeness, family comments, shame, weakness, and hypervigilance for someone entering the home. An explosion-specific trigger pulls toward a very different trauma context and is not supported by the memory, threat, or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm as a distraction strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the selected items. The maladaptive strategy set otherwise reflects avoidance and conflict-generation, while the connected nodes emphasize home intrusion vigilance, bodily reenactment, shame, weakness, and loss of trust. Because Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked to Triggers and somewhat to Threat/Negative Appraisals here, a severe self-injurious coping item stands out as insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and item pattern.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: 'Seeking Conflict' is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile. The patient's trauma is intimate partner physical abuse, and the other nodes describe hypervigilance, shame, weakness, loss of trust, and avoidance. Deliberately creating interpersonal conflict is a marked shift in style that is not supported by the accompanying threat, memory, appraisal, or trigger items, making this maladaptive strategy clinically incoherent in this profile.

vignette:
At age 74, Luisa still worked three mornings a week behind the counter of a small independent pharmacy in Miami, though she had long stopped believing that the work mattered the way it once had. The abuse had happened more than forty years ago, at the hands of a man she had loved and lived with for two years before she finally left. He had been charming at first—bringing her coffee, whispering that she was the only one who understood him—and then, slowly, the charm had turned to grip. The night she remembered most clearly, the night that still came to her as a series of frozen images, had started with a comment about her mother. He said her mother thought she was too good for him. She had tried to reassure him, but his face had changed, and then he had grabbed her by the shoulders and slammed her against the bedroom door. In the snapshot that always came first, she saw the wood grain of the door an inch from her nose, felt the shock run through her spine. Then another image: his hand around her throat, the pressure just enough to make her see stars, his voice saying she needed to learn respect. She had stayed frozen, arms at her sides, not fighting back, because she was certain that if she moved he would kill her. That position—back against the door, arms pressed to her ribs, chin tilted up—was exactly the position her body assumed now, involuntarily, whenever a memory surfaced. She would be standing at the pharmacy counter, handing a patient a bottle of blood-pressure medication, and then suddenly her shoulders would lock, her jaw would clench, and she would feel the door against her spine as though she were still there.

She had never told her husband, Carlos, the full story. Carlos was a gentle man, a retired bus driver who brought her tea every evening and asked about her day. But closeness with him had become a kind of minefield. When he came up behind her and wrapped his arms around her waist, she would stiffen. When he leaned in to kiss her cheek, she would turn her head away before she could stop herself. She knew he felt it, and she saw the hurt in his eyes, but what frightened her most was the feeling that if she let herself relax into his warmth, she would be betraying some ancient, essential vigilance. She had come to believe that she was no longer capable of the things that had once defined her: the easy laughter with customers, the pride she used to take in solving a tricky insurance problem, the sense of being useful. And deeper still, she had lost faith—faith that people could be trusted, that life held any fairness, that a higher power had ever been watching over her. As a girl she had prayed the rosary every night, believing God would protect the good. Now when she passed the little church on Calle Ocho she felt nothing but a hollow ache; if God existed, He had let that man put His hand around her throat. She no longer spoke to anyone about hope or redemption—those words felt like lies. At home, she could not sit with her back to a room. She arranged the couch so she faced the hallway. She noticed every creak of the floorboards, every click of the lock. The sound of a door opening—any door, the bathroom door, the pantry door, a car door outside—made her heart seize. She had stopped going to family gatherings months ago, because someone would inevitably make a comment about a cousin or an aunt, and the tone would be too close to his tone, and she would feel the snap of the memory.

The avoidance had crept in slowly, at first just a pattern of saying no to invitations. Then she began to avoid her own body. She stopped looking in the mirror when she undressed. She wore loose, dark clothing and did not let her hands touch her own skin when she showered. She learned to push feelings away before they could fully form—if she felt a wave of sadness while watching a movie, she would get up and start folding laundry. If she felt anger at a rude customer, she would swallow it until it turned into a dull ache behind her eyes. The consequence was that she had become a ghost in her own life. Carlos had started sleeping in the guest room because she flinched when he reached for her in the dark. Her daughter called less often because Luisa never answered the phone anymore. Last month, the pharmacy manager had asked if she was okay, and she had said yes, but she knew she looked brittle and exhausted. And every Sunday, when she used to light a candle at the church, she now stayed home, because she could not bear to ask for anything from a God who had already shown her that prayers were useless.

What finally brought her to seek help was a single moment: she was walking through the living room, and Carlos opened the front door to get the mail. The sound of the latch releasing sent her into a full-body freeze. She dropped to her knees, one hand raised in front of her face, and she stayed that way for almost a minute before she could breathe again. Carlos found her there, and for the first time, she did not turn away. She told him she needed to talk to someone. Now, sitting in the clinic, she is terrified that if she lets herself feel the shame that curls in her chest when she remembers how she did not fight back, she will finally understand that she is weak—the weak person she has always suspected she was. But she is also hoping, quietly, that maybe she can learn to sit with her back to a door again. And maybe, just maybe, she can find a way to believe in something again—in people, in life, in the possibility that the world is not only made of hands that grab and doors that slam.
